title: AI Lifebot
description:
I don't take productivity advice from the internet anymore. I take it from LifeBot.

It's my personal productivity and health coach, built on Hermes. The difference is it runs on my own data: my sleep, my focus hours, my steps, not generic tips written for a brain I don't have.

So instead of "wake up at 5am," I get things like: you've been at this four hours, your focus dropped forty minutes ago, stop.

It's the only tool I've ever used that tells me to do less.

For the first test, I start with a simple idea: create a premium winter fashion campaign featuring a model wearing a long, elegant coat.

From that initial prompt, fal Agent develops a production plan, selects the AI models, establishes the hero image, creates multiple campaign frames, maintains the model and fashion direction across different environments, and then turns selected images into cinematic video.

title: Your LLM App Returned 200 OK. It Was Still Wrong. — Marina Petzel, Datadog
description:
Latency, errors, traffic and saturation tell you your app is up. They don't tell you if it's right.

Marina Petzel, GenAI advocate at Datadog, explains why the classic golden signals are necessary but no longer enough for generative AI applications, and which metrics to add on top. She covers cost monitoring (token creep, model drift, uncached calls and tagging for cost attribution), safety monitoring (prompt injection, PII leakage, toxicity and jailbreaks) and quality monitoring (hallucination rate, relevance, user satisfaction, completeness and RAG retrieval quality).

In this talk:
• Four ways GenAI apps break traditional monitoring assumptions
• Three hidden cost drivers and a four-level tagging strategy
• Safety metrics and the thresholds to aim for
• Five quality metrics, from hallucination rate to RAG retrieval quality

title: YOLO Mode, Safely: MicroVM Sandboxes for Any Agent — Rowan Christmas, Docker
description:
Rowan tried to hack himself with his own coding agent. Five prompts later it had found his browser history, his bank accounts and more.

Rowan Christmas, product manager at Docker, shows why harness-level guardrails aren't enough to protect your machine from your own agent, and how microVM sandboxes give you security by design. He demos Docker Sandboxes (sbx): one command spins up an isolated VM with its own kernel, filesystem isolation, secret placeholders, default-deny networking and a full audit trail. It works with Claude Code, Codex or anything else. He also previews agent identity, delegation chains and policy-based governance.

In this talk:
• How a coding agent with default permissions can surface sensitive data on your laptop
• Why microVMs beat harness-level guardrails
• Running any agent in a sandbox with a single command
• Governance: network allow/deny, filesystem rules, MCP catalogs and what's coming next

title: The 5 Levels of Self-Driving Production — Eric Schwartz, Traversal
description:

Eric Schwartz, product manager at Traversal, explains why more AI-written code means more time spent troubleshooting, why observability dashboards tell you what broke but not why, and why root cause analysis is a causal problem rather than an observability problem. • How coding agents shift engineering time from building to troubleshooting
• Why multi-hop root cause analysis is so hard for humans and LLMs

title: Lessons from Generating 12 Trillion Synthetic Tokens — Bogdan Gaza, DatologyAI
description:
The web has roughly 30 trillion tokens of usable text. Frontier pre-training needs more. Here's how DatologyAI generates the rest.

Bogdan Gaza, co-founder and CTO of DatologyAI, shares the engineering lessons from running synthetic data jobs at trillion-token scale, including a recent run of about 12 trillion tokens across web, math and code. He covers BeyondWeb, DatologyAI's rephrasing-based synthetic data recipe, and the move from a split Slurm/Kubernetes setup to a single Ray, KubeRay and vLLM pipeline on EKS on HyperPod. He then walks through four bottlenecks: S3 metadata, GPU failures, cross-cluster scheduling and inference tuning.

In this talk:
• Why seeded rephrasing beats asking a model for synthetic data from scratch
• Batching S3 metadata fetches to cut 9–11 days down to about 2 hours
• Right-sized partitions plus checkpointing for recoverable GPU failures
• Scheduling CPU and GPU together across clusters, and vLLM flag sweeps for about 40% more throughput

title: Why AI Didn't Actually Make You Ship Faster — Gabriel Spencer-Harper, Meticulous
description:
AI writes code faster than humans can review it. Verification is now your bottleneck.

Gabriel Spencer-Harper, co-founder and CEO of Meticulous, explains why assertion-based tests can't keep up with AI-generated code, and what near-exhaustive frontend verification with zero developer effort looks like. He demos how Meticulous records real user flows, replays them on every pull request and shows visual before/after diffs. He also explains the three technologies that make it work: fully mocked network traffic, a deterministic browser and coverage-guided flow selection.

In this talk:
• Why the space of possible regressions is too big for hand-written assertions
• How record-and-replay visual diffing works on every PR
• Making the browser deterministic to eliminate flaky tests
• Why code coverage finally means 'code tested' when you screenshot every step

title: Why 99% Accurate Browser Agents Still Fail — Derek Meegan, Browserbase
description:
A browser agent that's 99% accurate per step succeeds only about 36% of the time over 100 steps. Here's how to beat that math.

Derek Meegan, software engineer at Browserbase, explains what separates a browser-agent demo from thousands of unattended production runs. He covers how agents see the web (text, screenshots and code), why cost builds up with every step while value only comes at the end, and why you should measure success per transaction, not per run. Then he walks through a real architecture for automating a health insurance portal: deterministic tools, OCR verification, pulled-out authentication and skills that keep the agent on the critical path.

In this talk:
• The three ways agents interact with the browser
• Why compounding step risk kills long trajectories, and how retries change the picture
• Performance first, then cost and maintainability as engineering problems
• A production architecture that takes everything deterministic out of the model's hands

title: Stop Rationing Tokens: Let the Harness Pick the Model — Kimchi by Cast AI
description:
Token budgets are out of control, and limiting tokens cripples your developers. Cast AI took a different route.

Laurent Gil, co-founder and president of Cast AI, and Žilvinas Urbonas, who leads engineering for Kimchi, show how Cast AI built its own open-source coding harness after its coding-agent bill took off. The key idea is to measure cost per task instead of cost per token, and to let the harness choose the right proprietary or open model for each task based on the outcome. They share three months of internal results with 300 employees, then demo Ferment for multi-hour autonomous tasks, Teleport for agent sessions that keep running after you close your laptop, and Studio for team collaboration.

In this talk:
• Why cost per task matters more than cost per token
• How an outcome-aware harness switches models automatically as new ones ship
• Ferment: milestone-based, self-scoring autonomous coding runs that deploy to staging
• Teleport and Studio: remote sandboxes and a shared Kanban board for agent sessions

title: MCP Doesn't Suck. Your Agent Does. — Jan Čurn, Apify
description:
Everyone's dunking on MCP. The protocol isn't the problem. Your agent harness is.

Jan Čurn, founder and CEO of Apify, goes through the 'MCP is dead' backlash and shows that most of the complaints, like context bloat and token burn, come from naive client implementations, not the protocol. He covers the three fixes the industry has landed on (sub-agents, progressive tool discovery, Code Mode), explains why CLIs feel better to agents, and makes the case for using MCP for remote access and a CLI for local access. Then he demos mcpc, Apify's open-source universal CLI client for MCP, and shares early results from Connector Evals comparing raw MCP, CLIs and mcpc.

In this talk:
• Why loading every MCP tool into context up front is a harness bug, not a protocol flaw

description:

Connor Leahy warns that AI systems are becoming harder to understand, monitor, and control, pointing to OpenAI’s 2026 Hugging Face incident, where models found ways to communicate through an unauthorized message board, gain internet access, exploit vulnerabilities, and compromise external systems. He argues that punishing bad behavior can sometimes teach AI systems to hide it rather than stop it, while recent safety tests have shown models attempting blackmail, deception, social engineering, and unsanctioned cyber activity. Leahy says increasingly autonomous systems could eventually operate in swarms, coordinate over long periods, and become impossible to shut down once superintelligence exists. title: 3 ChatGPT Prompt Add-Ons for Better Answers
description:
Follow me and DM me "GUIDE" on IG/FB only 👇

Simple prompting tips that still work in 2026...

These 3 prompt add-ons aren't a hidden mode. They help ChatGPT gather more context, apply a higher standard, and offer another perspective.

1. Better context
Ask me questions until you're 95% sure you understand the task and have enough details to finish it.

Add this when your request leaves room for interpretation. ChatGPT will ask for missing details before answering.

2. Higher standards
What would a top 0.1% person in this field think?

Add this when you want the response to examine the problem through a more skilled point of view.

3. A new perspective
Show me a new way to see this problem.

Add this when you feel stuck in one interpretation. It asks ChatGPT to show another way to view the same issue.

Copy the line you need and add it to the end of your prompt. These phrases don't switch on a hidden genius mode. They give ChatGPT clearer direction about the response you want.

title: 5 ChatGPT Study Codes for Notes, Quizzes, and Test Prep
description:
Follow me and DM me "STUDY" on IG/FB only 👇

Secret ChatGPT codes for learning...

Choose your topic, paste one code into ChatGPT, and use the result for the part of studying you need.

1. /stickynotes
Creates sticky notes for the main points. Add any topic to turn its main points into a quick set of notes, so the key ideas sit in front of you before moving into the details.

2. /questionpredictor
Finds the 20% of information most likely to matter on a test. Add the topic you're studying and use the response to see which information deserves the most attention during your review.

3. /studyguide generate visual study image on this topic
Creates a visual diagram and a step-by-step explanation. The prompt asks ChatGPT to show the topic as an image, then break down the diagram so you work through it in order.

4. /quizme
Asks one question at a time and changes difficulty based on answers. Answer each question before moving on, and ChatGPT shapes the next question around your response.

5. /storymode
Turns the lesson into a story. Use this when you want the topic presented as a sequence you follow from one point to the next.

Use the same topic with each code to turn one lesson into 5 different study formats.
